Why this allocation?

Make the trade-offs explicit

Our constrained mean–variance model maximizes estimated return at an 8% volatility target. Position limits and minimum exposures are policy choices supplied to the model.

Look beyond capital weights

SPY and DBC each account for approximately 40% of estimated risk. STIP has the largest capital weight, but contributes about 6.24% of risk. This is not a risk-parity portfolio.

Keep a short-duration bond allocation

VGSH and STIP together receive 34.05% of capital. The model requires at least 20% across these two ETFs; their final combined weight is an optimization result.

Inputs, constraints and source data

Estimates use 60 monthly USD returns, October 2021–September 2026. The portfolio is long only and unlevered, with a 35% capital cap per ETF, a 40% risk-share cap per ETF and a 65% combined equity risk-share cap. Additional minimum exposures are documented in the methodology.

The latest revalidation uses Bloomberg ETF prices and a separate FRED DGS1MO risk-free yield-accrual proxy. The agreed weights pass the independently recalculated capital and risk-limit checks. Share quantities and execution prices are not included here. Read the original methodology and public-data code

The six ETFs

What each ETF brings to the portfolio

Our Round 1 allocation combines equities, commodities and short-term bonds. Here’s how each ETF fits in.

SPYUS equities · Broad market

Broad US equity exposure

SPY gives us exposure to large US companies across sectors. It is one of the main drivers of both expected return and estimated risk in the portfolio.

EEMVEmerging-market equities · Minimum volatility

Equities beyond the US

EEMV adds emerging-market equities through a minimum-volatility strategy. It broadens our geographical exposure, although it still carries equity and currency risk.

DBCCommodities · Futures-based

Commodity exposure

DBC adds a basket of commodity futures to the portfolio. It gives us exposure beyond equities and bonds, but also accounts for a large share of estimated risk. Its returns depend partly on the cost or benefit of rolling futures contracts.

SCHDUS equities · Dividend-focused

Dividend-focused US equities

SCHD adds a dividend-focused allocation alongside SPY. The two funds overlap in their US equity exposure, so we assess their risk together.

VGSHBonds · Short-term US Treasuries

Short-term government bonds

VGSH holds short-term US Treasuries. It forms part of our lower-risk bond allocation and is less sensitive to interest-rate changes than longer-term bonds, although its price can still fluctuate.

STIPBonds · Short-term US TIPS

Inflation-linked government bonds

STIP holds short-term US inflation-protected Treasuries. It adds inflation-linked exposure alongside VGSH, but can still lose value when real yields rise.

Round 1 / Decision journal

How we arrived at the allocation

What we chose, the trade-offs we accepted and what we want to revisit.

  1. Risk target

    Working with an 8% volatility target

    We set an 8% annual volatility target, with limits on how much capital and risk any one ETF can account for. The optimizer then finds weights within those limits. The limits are our inputs to the model, rather than results it produces.

  2. Risk concentration

    Most of the risk comes from SPY and DBC

    Although we allocate capital across six ETFs, SPY and DBC account for most of the estimated risk. The short-term bonds take up a sizeable share of the portfolio’s capital but contribute relatively little to its risk.

  3. Comparisons

    Checking against equal weight and risk parity

    We also tested equal-weight and risk-parity allocations. Our allocation’s historical Sharpe ratio was only slightly higher than equal weight. Risk parity had much lower volatility, so its lower return needs to be read in that context.

  4. Next review

    What we’ll revisit at the next rebalance

    At the next rebalance, we want to see whether we can reduce our reliance on SPY and DBC for risk. We’ll look at how potential positions move alongside the existing holdings, rather than assume that adding more names will make the portfolio more diversified.

    Until then, that concentration remains a limitation of the allocation.

Why these tickers aren’t in the portfolio

VWO and XLE were both in the earlier dataset, but they were left out at different stages.

VWO Included in the model, but given no weight

We kept VWO in the seven-ETF universe. With our inputs and constraints, the optimizer assigned it no weight, leaving EEMV as our emerging-market holding. Different assumptions could lead to a different result.

XLE Removed before running the model

We removed XLE to avoid a separate energy-sector equity position alongside our broader holdings. In the earlier public-data comparison, reoptimizing without XLE produced broadly comparable historical performance, with no demonstrated performance penalty. That supported dropping the extra sector tilt while keeping the other ETF choices available. DBC still includes energy commodities, so this does not remove all energy exposure.

Historical research, not live performance.

The final weights were fitted using data that overlap this backtest. ETF and model selection also used historical results, so this is not an untouched out-of-sample test. The Sharpe advantage over equal weight is modest, and the risk-parity comparison has a substantially lower risk level.

Risk analysis / One-month horizon

Value at Risk

How large could a bad month be? We look at the 95% loss threshold in two ways: the historical backtest and a normal model of the allocation.

Historical estimate

3.68% of portfolio value

The loss threshold taken from the fifth percentile of net monthly backtest returns, including simulated trading costs.

Based on the backtest’s monthly outcomes

Normal-model estimate

3.80% of portfolio value

The estimated one-month loss threshold using the allocation’s volatility and a zero-mean normal return assumption.

Based on estimated volatility and a distribution assumption

95% confidence does not mean a loss limit. VaR describes a threshold with a 5% lower tail under the relevant distribution. Losses beyond it can be much larger; neither estimate tells us how severe those losses would be.

View VaR formulas and assumptions

Historical VaR95% = −Q0.05(Rt)

Normal VaR95%, monthly ≈ 1.645 × σannual / √12

R is the net monthly backtest return. Q is its fifth percentile. The normal-model estimate uses annualized allocation volatility and assumes zero mean. Values are approximate; these two methods use different inputs.

Methodology

How we calculated the results

The five steps below connect the price data to the allocation and backtest. Open each formula for the notation and definitions.

  1. Estimate the inputs. Convert the supplied month-end USD prices into simple monthly returns: current price divided by previous price, minus one. Multiply the mean monthly return and monthly sample covariance by 12 to obtain annual inputs. The estimation window contains 60 complete returns; adjustment provenance is explained below.
    View formulas and definitions

    ri,t = Pi,t / Pi,t−1 − 1

    μ = 12 × mean(rt)   ·   Σ = 12 × Cov(rt)

    P is the month-end price; r is the monthly return. μ and Σ are the annualized mean-return vector and sample covariance matrix.
  2. Choose the weights. Maximize estimated annual return at an 8% estimated volatility target, subject to the capital and risk-share limits. Multiple numerical starting points check stability; they do not prove a global optimum.
    View formulas and definitions

    maximizew   wᵀμ

    σp = √(wᵀΣw) = 0.08

    Risk sharei = wi(Σw)i / (wᵀΣw)

    w contains the ETF capital weights. The optimization also applies the capital and risk-share limits described above.
  3. Freeze the allocation for the backtest. Restore the same target weights every month after market movements. This test does not re-optimize the portfolio at each rebalance.
    View formulas and definitions

    gt = ∑i wiri,t

    w̃i,t = wi(1 + ri,t−1) / (1 + gt−1)

    g is the gross monthly portfolio return. w̃ is the drifted weight before the next rebalance; the target w stays fixed.
  4. Deduct trading costs. Model trading costs at 10 basis points times the sum of absolute target-minus-drifted weights, including the initial investment. Net return is (1 − cost × turnover) × (1 + gross return) − 1. This proportional-cost convention measures turnover before deducting fees; it is not a trade-by-trade execution model.
    View formulas and definitions

    Tt = ∑i |wi − w̃i,t|

    Rt = (1 − 0.001 × Tt)(1 + gt) − 1

    T counts purchases and sales; 0.001 is 10 basis points. At inception, ETF weights before trading are zero, so T = 1. R is the return after costs.
  5. Measure the outcome. Compound net monthly returns for CAGR and month-end drawdown. Annualize monthly volatility by the square root of 12. Sharpe uses annualized mean monthly excess return divided by annualized portfolio volatility.
    View formulas and definitions

    Vt = Vt−1(1 + Rt)

    CAGR = (VN / V0)12/N − 1

    σannual = √12 × s(R)

    Sharpe = 12 × mean(Rt − rf,t) / σannual

    Max. drawdown = mint [Vt / max0≤s≤t Vs − 1]

    V is portfolio value, N is the number of months, s(R) is the sample standard deviation and rf,t is the monthly risk-free proxy. Drawdown includes the initial value and month-end observations.
Data sources and limitations

The Bloomberg workbook visibly confirms dividend and split adjustment settings for SPY. Other ETF columns contain saved values, so their original request settings cannot be confirmed directly. Their returns were compared with the prior adjusted-price series, with small differences. The risk-free input remains a Treasury yield-accrual proxy, not an observed T-bill total-return index.

The downloadable results below come from the rerun using Bloomberg ETF prices and the agreed weights. The original repository contains the earlier public-data analysis, whose headline figures agree at the precision displayed here.
